sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Origin of Dual Government (1765)**: Conceived by **Robert Clive** after the Treaty of Allahabad; Company acquired **Diwani** rights directly from Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, while **Nizamat** remained nominally with the Nawab of Bengal.
• **Irresponsible Power**: The Company exercised all real economic and military power without administrative accountability, leaving the Indian officials responsible for law and order without adequate financial resources.
• **Disastrous Economic Impact**: Unchecked extortion by Company officials, famine of **1770 (Chabbisi Manthan)**, and massive ruin of Bengal’s agrarian and traditional handicraft economy.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: By 1772, Bengal's treasury was in chronic deficit despite high revenue extraction due to rampant corruption and private trade monopolies.

items.definition: The right to collect land revenue and administer civil justice, granted to the East India Company by the Mughal Emperor in 1765.
The executive, military, and criminal administration of the province, nominally retained by the Nawab of Bengal under the Dual System.
The London-based governing body of the East India Company that ordered Warren Hastings to abolish the Dual System and 'stand forth as diwan'.
The Regulating Act of 1773, Revenue Boards established by Warren Hastings, and the shifting of the treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Bengal Presidency Hubs**: Murshidabad (former administrative capital), Calcutta (new center of Company power and treasury), Dhaka, and Patna.
• **Driving Advantages**: Fertile Gangetic delta, robust pre-existing trade networks, and strategic coastal access facilitating British export of Indian textiles and opium.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Dual accountability vacuum, rampant private trade abuse by Company servants, and severe famines.
• **Policy Interventions**: Warren Hastings abolished the office of the Naib Diwan, centralized revenue collection under British collectors, and relocated the capital to Calcutta.

items.title: Mnemonic for Bengal Administrative Evolution
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "Clive Created, Hastings Halted"
• **Decoded Meaning**: Robert Clive instituted the Dual System in 1765; Warren Hastings abolished it in 1772.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly prevents chronological confusion between the introduction and abolition phases.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: 1765 (Dual System Starts) -> 1770 (Bengal Famine) -> 1772 (Dual System Ends & Hastings takes charge) -> 1773 (Regulating Act).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently misleads candidates by stating that the Dual System was abolished by the Regulating Act of 1773. In reality, Warren Hastings abolished the Dual System administratively in 1772, prior to the passage of the Regulating Act in 1773.

Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'irresponsible power' when analyzing the Dual System. Highlight how the separation of economic extraction from administrative welfare created institutional decay, culminating in the 1770 Famine.

keyTakeaways: The Dual System separated Diwani and Nizamat, creating a regime of unchecked power without responsibility.
Warren Hastings abolished the Dual System in 1772, moving the East India Company to openly take direct charge of revenue and administration.
The abolition laid the groundwork for centralized British rule and paved the way for the Regulating Act of 1773.
